TRAM flap

Six animal reports generally found greater TRAM-flap survival or less necrosis after PBM, with increases in perfusion-related measures. Doses and spectra differed, and one comparison favored ultrasound over PBM.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Six animal reports generally found greater TRAM-flap survival or less necrosis after PBM, with increases in perfusion-related measures. Doses and spectra differed, and one comparison favored ultrasound over PBM.

Summary of the Evidence

Six animal publications directly examined transverse rectus abdominis musculocutaneous, or TRAM, flap viability. Four are filed under the specific TRAM-flap category, while two matching experiments are listed under the broader skin-flap category. They comprise five rat and one mouse study from Brazil and Turkey. These papers are a focused subset of the larger skin-flap literature, not six human studies or six different reconstructive settings. No human or independent cell-culture study of PBM for TRAM-flap survival was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical study was identified in which PBM was used to improve TRAM-flap survival in patients. The evidence described here concerns experimental surgical flaps in rodents.

Animal evidence

Across the six reports, PBM commonly reduced measured necrosis or increased flap viability. In diabetic rats, a 660-nm red-light protocol at 140 J/cm² performed better than 10 J/cm² on several outcomes, including necrotic area and leukocyte count; mast cells, epidermal thickness, VEGF, FGF, and new vessels increased. That experiment also included pulsed electrical-field treatment, so its combined-treatment findings should not all be attributed to light alone (Leite et al. 2017).

In nicotine-exposed rats, 830-nm near-infrared PBM was associated with smaller necrotic areas and greater flap viability, alongside increased mast-cell counts and VEGF and CD34 expression. Separate 670-nm red-light experiments reported reduced necrosis or greater angiogenesis and VEGF, although the protocols and exposure schedules differed (das Neves et al. 2016; Pinfildi et al. 2009; Pinfildi et al. 2013).

The mapped mouse experiment found that both PBM and therapeutic ultrasound maintained flap viability, but ultrasound had greater potential on the measured comparison. A rat experiment using polychromatic light also reported increased survival in the TRAM model, though the exposure details were incompletely reported (Canever et al. 2021; Calis et al. 2019).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols included 660- and 670-nm red visible light, 830-nm near-infrared light, and polychromatic light spanning approximately 590 to 1500 nm. Reported fluences ranged from 6 to 144 J/cm² in one protocol; a diabetic-rat comparison favored 140 over 10 J/cm². A mouse comparison used 830-nm light at 5 J/cm². Timing and application sites varied, and the polychromatic study omitted key dosimetry. These experiments do not establish a preferred dose for human breast reconstruction.

Interpretation

The animal reports generally found higher flap viability or less necrosis, with accompanying changes in vascular and growth-factor measures. The results are favorable within rodent TRAM models but come from varied protocols, and ultrasound performed better in one comparison. Clinical benefit in people has not been tested.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)Low-to-moderate for greater TRAM-flap viability in animal models

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Six rat and mouse publications include four indexed under TRAM flap and two matching TRAM experiments under the broader skin-flap category. Most report smaller necrotic areas or greater viability, perfusion, or angiogenesis, but protocols vary and one comparison favored ultrasound. Replication by independent teams using prespecified flap-survival measures would strengthen confidence in this animal result.
